post_content:
By 2027, India will create 2.3 million AI jobs.

There is just one problem: we may only have 1.2 million people qualified to fill them.

According to NASSCOM and BCG, India's AI market will triple to over $17 billion (₹1.45 lakh crore) by 2027. The momentum looks undeniable:

→ 92% of Indian knowledge workers use GenAI at work (vs. 72% globally).
→ India ranks #1 worldwide in AI skill penetration.
→ The ₹10,000 crore IndiaAI Mission is backing this with 10,000+ national GPUs.

Yet beneath the headline growth lies a strategic paradox.

While we lead the world in adoption, India ranks #89 out of 109 in deep technical proficiency.

We are exceptional at consuming applications, but underrepresented in building foundational models and core IP. As the industry pivots from basic GenAI to complex agentic architectures, knowing how to write prompts won't safeguard high-value tech roles.

The real test for India in 2027 isn't whether we spend $17 billion on software.

It is whether we build the intellectual property ourselves, or simply pay rent on compute and models engineered elsewhere.

To bridge the looming 1.1-million talent deficit, our tech ecosystem must pivot immediately from routine implementation to foundational engineering.

Can India transition from the world's digital back office to the world's AI factory by 2027?

I’d love to hear your perspective below.

India has 170 medical AI startups. Exactly 4 have crossed Series B.

Funding rebounded sharply to $206M in 2025, and projections suggest the market will surge tenfold to $4.77B by 2034. On paper, the sector looks like a breakout success.

In reality, over 90% of Indian healthtech AI is trapped in "pilot purgatory."

Here is the uncomfortable truth: India doesn't have an algorithm crisis. We have a plumbing crisis.

Venture capital is racing to fund clinical foundation models, yet overlooking the baseline reality of healthcare delivery:

→ Over 1.19 billion health records are linked via national ABDM rails.
→ Yet hospital EMR adoption remains stuck at roughly 35%.
→ Nearly two-thirds of clinical documentation outside metro hospital chains is still recorded on paper.

You cannot deploy scalable, multi-modal diagnostic AI when foundational workflows aren't even digitized.

Combine this with high clinical validation costs and a lack of clear reimbursement pathways from insurers, and the scaling math collapses before Series A.

The real winners in Indian medical AI won't be the teams with the flashiest models. They will be the ones unglamorous enough to fix the workflow infrastructure and deliver measurable enterprise ROI to hospital administrators.

Are we building medical AI for the reality of Indian healthcare delivery—or just for demo days?

I’d love to hear your thoughts.

topic: travel to vanuatu 2026 as indian passpost holder
post_content:
Last week, a founder friend of mine was venting about his third visa rejection of the year.

Piles of financial statements, weeks of waiting, and nothing to show for it except non-refundable flight credits.

I asked him: "Have you ever looked at Vanuatu?"

He stared at me blankly. "Where even is that?"

Here is something most Indian travelers completely overlook:

In 2026, while people fight for stressful 15-day embassy slots, Vanuatu quietly allows Indian passport holders to enter completely visa-free for 120 days.

That’s four whole months. No embassy interview. No bank audits. Just a passport and a boarding pass to the South Pacific.

It is one of the longest visa-free stay allowances granted to Indian citizens anywhere in the world—far beyond the typical 30-day tourist stamp.

Our passport now grants access to around 70 destinations via visa-free, visa-on-arrival, or eTA agreements. Yet we keep returning to the same three overcrowded weekend getaways.

Maybe the real travel unlock isn’t waiting for approval from countries making it harder each year.

It’s choosing places that welcome you with open arms.

If you had a 4-month open ticket to live and work by the Pacific, would you take it? Or is Bali still your default?
